title: The renouncer who keeps working
hook: Arjuna asks which is better, quitting or working, and Krishna redraws the renouncer
carry: karma yoga: drop the fruit, not the work

segments.voice: Yesterday's line: dharma lives at an honest counter too. At his market stall, Tuladhara held the same even scale for everyone, and taught an ascetic with birds in his hair.

On the battlefield of Kurukshetra, Arjuna has already said he'd rather live on a beggar's alms than fight. Krishna has praised both letting go and action, and Arjuna is confused. At the start of chapter five he asks: you praise giving up action, and you praise the yoga of action. Tell me for certain which one is better. Krishna's answer: both lead to the highest, but of the two, the yoga of action is better. Hindu tradition honors the sannyasi, the renouncer who gives up home, possessions and the household fire. And a chapter later, Krishna redraws who counts as one.
screen: `ARJUNA: I'D RATHER BEG.` → `WHICH IS BETTER?` → `THE YOGA OF ACTION.`

segments.voice: Here's the verse that opens chapter six, in paraphrase. The one who does the work that ought to be done, without leaning on its fruit, is a renouncer, and a yogi. Not the one who has merely put out the fire. Not the one who has merely stopped acting. Take it in pieces. The work that ought to be done: in Sanskrit, karyam karma. The work that's actually yours to do, today. Without leaning on its fruit: the word is anashritah, not taking shelter in, not propping yourself up on. The fruit is the result: the praise, the raise, the thank-you. The verse doesn't say results don't matter. It says don't lean your whole weight on them. And the fire: commentators read it as the household's sacred fires, which a renouncer no longer tends. Putting out the fire doesn't make you free; letting go inwardly does. The next verse makes it plain: what people call renunciation, Krishna says, know that to be yoga. This is karma yoga, the path of action, one of the great paths of Hinduism: your own work, offered, without clinging to its fruit. Yesterday a merchant held his scale level in a crowded market. Today Krishna tells a warrior the deepest letting go can happen without leaving the field. Read this way, the Gita leaves room for a nurse, a farmer or a clerk to renounce too, without leaving the work.
screen: `THE WORK THAT OUGHT TO BE DONE.` · `NOT LEANING ON THE FRUIT.` · `PUTTING OUT THE FIRE ISN'T THE THING.` · `KARMA YOGA: A RENOUNCER WHO KEEPS WORKING.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one piece of work waiting for you and notice the fruit you're leaning on, the reply, the approval, the result, and where that leaning lives in the body, maybe the shoulders, maybe the jaw. On each out-breath, shift your weight back onto your own two feet: the work is still there and you still care how it goes, you're just not hanging on it. If you pray, you can offer the result to God and keep the work.
Seva as vocation. In the Gita's sixth chapter, the renouncer is the one who does the work that's theirs, without leaning on its fruit.
Your line: karma yoga: drop the fruit, not the work. The renouncer isn't defined by the robe or the cabin. Back tomorrow, same hill.

howItsDone: Hindu teachers of karma yoga turn to the opening of the Gita's sixth chapter to explain that renunciation can be practiced inwardly, by letting go of the fruit of action while continuing to work.
